outputs.L1:
(CNN) — Pakistan’s former president said his country is being treated “unequally” compared with other nations, despite being a staunch ally of the United States in its war on terror.

Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf said anti-American sentiment in Pakistan remains high.

“Pakistan is being treated so unequally while we are the ones who are in the lead role fighting the global war on terror,” Musharraf said in an interview with CNN’s Wolf Blitzer for *The Situation Room*. “This is what hurts Pakistan. It hurts the leadership. Indeed, it hurts the government. It hurts the people of Pakistan.”

Musharraf spoke from Dallas, Texas, while on a book tour in the United States. The interview took place amid reports Friday of U.S. drone strikes on militant targets in Pakistan, just days after the start of the Obama administration, which has made combating al Qaeda and Taliban militants in Pakistan’s tribal region near Afghanistan its most immediate national security priority.

Asked whether he was comfortable with the continuation of the attacks, even under a new U.S. president, Musharraf said: “Nobody in Pakistan is comfortable with the strikes across the border. There is no doubt in that. Public opinion is very much against it.

“But as far as this issue of the new president — President Obama having taken over and this continuing — I have always been saying that policies don’t change with personalities; policies have national interest, and policies depend on an environment.

“So the environment and national interest of the United States being the same, I thought policies will remain constant,” he said.

Musharraf also addressed a statement he had made about the $10 billion in assistance Pakistan has received from the United States, describing it as a “pittance for a country which is in the lead role to fight terrorism.”

He emphasized his gratitude to the United States for the funding, but said the amount was small compared with the billions spent in Afghanistan and “maybe over a trillion dollars” in Iraq.

“Please don’t think that this $10 billion was such a great amount that we ought to be eternally grateful while we know that we deserve much more and we should have got much more and we must get much more if we are to fight the global war on terror,” he said.

Musharraf stressed that Pakistan had been “in the lead role fighting a war for you for 10 years, between ’79 and ’89,” referring to Pakistan’s alliance with the United States and the Afghan mujahedeen rebels during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.

He emphasized that, for 42 years up until 1989, Pakistan had been a “strategic partner” of the United States. But many Pakistanis felt abandoned by the United States after the Russians withdrew from Afghanistan. Musharraf said the 1989 “peace dividend” went to Europe — Eastern Europe. Pakistan was “left alone” from 1989 to 2001, and during that period, the militant Taliban movement took control of Afghanistan.

“What did Pakistan get out of fighting for 10 years with you? Nothing, sir,” he said, explaining why public opinion in Pakistan has been “so much against the United States.”

Musharraf said public opinion in his country is strongly opposed to U.S. drone strikes against militants in Pakistan’s tribal region. While al Qaeda and the Taliban must be confronted, he said, “public opinion is certainly against the methodology being adopted.”

Musharraf, once Pakistan’s army chief, resigned under intense political pressure in August as the ruling coalition began taking steps to impeach him. He had swept to power in 1999 in a bloodless coup.

Asked why al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, who was thought to be somewhere in the border region, had not been found, Musharraf replied:

“I would like to ask the United States why he hasn’t been found. They have their intelligence. You have more intelligence capability. I would like to ask the United States why Mullah Omar has not been found, who is the leader of all of the Taliban in Afghanistan?”

Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf said anti-U.S. feeling in Pakistan is widespread.

“Pakistan is being treated so unequally while we are the ones who are in the lead role fighting the global war on terror,” Musharraf told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer during an interview for “The Situation Room.”

“That is what causes pain in Pakistan. It pains the leadership. It certainly pains the government. It pains the Pakistani people,” Musharraf said from Dallas, Texas, where he was appearing during a U.S. book tour.

The interview came as reports emerged Friday that American drones had hit militant targets inside Pakistan, only days after President Barack Obama’s administration began. The new administration had made the fight against al Qaeda and Taliban militants in Pakistan’s tribal areas along the Afghan border its most urgent national security concern.

Musharraf was asked whether he was at ease with the strikes continuing under a new U.S. president.

“No one in Pakistan is comfortable with attacks across the border. There is no question about that. Public opinion is strongly opposed to them,” he said.

“But regarding the issue of the new president — President Obama coming into office and this continuing — I have always said that policies do not change because of individuals. Policies are shaped by national interests, and they depend on circumstances.

“So, since the circumstances and the national interests of the United States remain the same, I believed the policies would stay the same,” he said.

Musharraf also discussed earlier remarks he had made about the $10 billion in U.S. aid Pakistan had received, describing it as a “pittance for a country which is in the lead role to fight terrorism.”

He said he was grateful to the United States for the money, but argued that the sum was small when compared with the billions spent in Afghanistan and “maybe over a trillion dollars” in Iraq.

“Please do not think this $10 billion was such a huge sum that we should be forever thankful, when we know we deserve far more, should have received far more, and must receive far more if we are to fight the global war on terror,” he said.

Musharraf underlined that Pakistan had been “in the lead role fighting a war for you for 10 years, between ’79 and ’89,” referring to Pakistan’s partnership with the United States and Afghan mujahedeen fighters during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan.

He also noted that for 42 years, until 1989, Pakistan had served as a “strategic partner” of the United States. However, he said many Pakistanis believed the United States deserted them after Soviet forces withdrew from Afghanistan.

According to Musharraf, the “peace dividend” after 1989 went to Europe — specifically Eastern Europe. Pakistan, he said, was “left alone” between 1989 and 2001, during which time the Taliban militant movement gained control of Afghanistan.

“What did Pakistan receive after fighting alongside you for 10 years? Nothing, sir,” he said, explaining why Pakistani public opinion had become “so much against the United States.”

Musharraf said people in Pakistan strongly oppose U.S. drone attacks on militants in the country’s tribal region. Although al Qaeda and the Taliban have to be fought, he said, “public opinion is certainly against the methodology being adopted.”

Musharraf, who was once Pakistan’s army chief, stepped down in August under heavy political pressure as the governing coalition began moving toward impeaching him. He had taken power in 1999 through a bloodless coup.

When asked why al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, believed to be hiding somewhere in the border area, had not been located, Musharraf answered:

“I would like to ask the United States why he has not been found. They have their intelligence. You have greater intelligence capabilities. I would also like to ask the United States why Mullah Omar has not been found — the leader of all the Taliban in Afghanistan.”

**Musharraf: Pakistan treated unfairly by U.S. despite terror fight**

**DALLAS** — Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf said Pakistan has been treated unequally by the United States despite making major sacrifices as a key ally in the war on terror, speaking in an interview with CNN’s Wolf Blitzer in Dallas.

Musharraf argued that Washington has often failed to recognize Pakistan’s role in combating extremist groups along the Afghan border and within its own territory.

“Pakistan has suffered enormously,” Musharraf said, pointing to military casualties, terrorist attacks and political instability he said were tied to the country’s cooperation with the United States after the September 11 attacks.

The former military ruler said Pakistan is frequently judged more harshly than other U.S. partners, particularly when questions arise over militant safe havens, intelligence cooperation and relations with Afghanistan.

His remarks come amid longstanding tensions between Washington and Islamabad over counterterrorism strategy, U.S. aid, drone strikes and Pakistan’s relationship with militant networks operating in the region.

Blitzer pressed Musharraf on criticism that elements inside Pakistan’s security establishment have tolerated or supported extremist groups. Musharraf rejected the accusation, saying Pakistan’s army and intelligence services have been on the front lines of the conflict.

He said the United States should treat Pakistan as a strategic partner rather than a subordinate ally, arguing that stability in South Asia depends on cooperation, not public blame.

Musharraf, who ruled Pakistan from 1999 to 2008 after taking power in a military coup, was a central figure in the U.S.-led campaign against al Qaeda and the Taliban following 9/11. His government allowed U.S. forces access to Pakistani airspace and logistical routes, decisions that were deeply controversial inside Pakistan.

He also defended his record in office, saying he made difficult choices under intense domestic and international pressure.

The interview in Dallas highlighted a familiar message from Musharraf: that Pakistan’s partnership with the United States came at a high cost, and that Washington has not always acknowledged the extent of those costs.

**Musharraf Says U.S. Drone Strikes Fuel Anti-American Sentiment but Pakistan Must Remain Allied With Washington**

Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf said in a CNN interview that U.S. drone strikes inside Pakistan have intensified anti-American feeling among Pakistanis and complicated Islamabad’s relationship with Washington, even as he argued that Pakistan and the United States remain strategically dependent on one another.

Musharraf criticized the drone campaign as politically damaging and deeply unpopular in Pakistan. He said the strikes are widely viewed by Pakistanis as violations of national sovereignty, particularly when they cause civilian casualties or are carried out without clear public approval from Pakistani authorities. According to Musharraf, the attacks may kill militants, but they also create anger that extremist groups can exploit.

He said anti-American sentiment in Pakistan is not simply the result of propaganda, but is tied to concrete grievances, including drone operations, civilian deaths, and the perception that the United States acts unilaterally inside Pakistani territory. Musharraf argued that such resentment weakens the ability of Pakistani leaders to cooperate openly with Washington, because any government seen as too close to the United States risks losing public legitimacy.

At the same time, Musharraf rejected the idea that Pakistan should abandon its alliance with the United States. He said the two countries have shared security interests, particularly in fighting terrorism and stabilizing the region. Pakistan, he argued, has suffered heavily from extremism and cannot afford to isolate itself from a major power like the United States.

Musharraf also suggested that the relationship has often suffered from mistrust on both sides. He said Washington has sometimes failed to appreciate Pakistan’s internal pressures and sacrifices, while Pakistan has had to balance cooperation with the United States against domestic anger over American military actions.

His remarks reflected the broader tension in U.S.-Pakistan relations: cooperation against militant groups alongside sharp disagreement over drone strikes, sovereignty, and public opinion. Musharraf portrayed Pakistan as an essential U.S. partner, but warned that tactics seen as heavy-handed or unilateral could strengthen anti-American forces and make the alliance harder to sustain.

**Musharraf criticizes U.S. aid policy, drone strikes in CNN interview**

*By CNN Staff*  
*Washington (CNN) —* Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf criticized the United States’ approach to Pakistan in an interview on CNN’s *The Situation Room*, saying Washington’s aid policies and drone campaign have fueled resentment and undermined cooperation between the two countries.

Speaking with Wolf Blitzer, Musharraf pushed back against U.S. criticism of Pakistan following the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, while acknowledging that bin Laden’s ability to live for years inside Pakistan represented a serious failure.

“The failure is there,” Musharraf said, referring to Pakistan’s inability to locate the al Qaeda leader before U.S. Navy SEALs found him in Abbottabad. But he rejected suggestions that Pakistani officials knowingly sheltered bin Laden, arguing that incompetence or intelligence lapses should not be equated with complicity.

Bin Laden was killed in May 2011 in a U.S. raid on a compound near Pakistan’s premier military academy, a discovery that intensified suspicions in Washington about whether elements inside Pakistan’s security establishment had protected him. Pakistani officials have repeatedly denied any official involvement.

Musharraf, who led Pakistan from 1999 to 2008 and was a key U.S. ally after the September 11 attacks, said the relationship between the two countries has deteriorated because of mistrust on both sides.

He sharply criticized the way U.S. assistance to Pakistan is discussed in Washington, saying aid is too often portrayed as a favor rather than as part of a strategic partnership. He argued that public threats to cut or condition assistance are counterproductive and humiliating to Pakistanis.

“When you talk of aid in a manner that insults Pakistan, you create a reaction,” Musharraf said in substance, emphasizing that Pakistan has suffered thousands of casualties in its fight against terrorism and should be treated with respect.

Musharraf also condemned U.S. drone strikes in Pakistan’s tribal areas, saying they violate Pakistani sovereignty and inflame anti-American sentiment, even when they kill militant leaders. The United States has long defended drone strikes as an effective tool against al Qaeda and Taliban-linked militants operating near the Afghan border, but Pakistani leaders have publicly objected to them.

The former president said unilateral American military actions make it harder for Pakistan’s government and armed forces to maintain public support for cooperation with the United States. He argued that counterterrorism efforts should be coordinated with Pakistani authorities rather than carried out without Islamabad’s approval.

The interview came amid continuing tensions over Pakistan’s role in the fight against extremism, the future of U.S. operations in Afghanistan, and congressional scrutiny of billions of dollars in American aid to Islamabad.

Musharraf said both countries still need each other, but he warned that the relationship cannot improve unless Washington recognizes Pakistan’s security concerns and Pakistan addresses the failures that allowed bin Laden to remain undetected.

“The trust deficit has to be removed,” he said, calling for a relationship based on mutual interests rather than public accusations.

# Musharraf says Pakistan deserves more U.S. support in fight against terrorism

**By CNN Staff**  
**Islamabad, Pakistan —** Former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf said Pakistan has not received enough recognition or support from the United States for its role in fighting terrorism, arguing that Islamabad has paid a heavy price as a key U.S. ally.

Musharraf, who led Pakistan from 1999 to 2008, said the country suffered thousands of casualties and significant economic damage while confronting militant groups along its border with Afghanistan and inside Pakistan.

“Pakistan has done more than most countries in the fight against terrorism,” Musharraf said. “The United States must understand the sacrifices Pakistan has made and provide support that reflects that reality.”

Pakistan became a central partner in Washington’s counterterrorism campaign after the September 11, 2001, attacks. The alliance brought billions of dollars in U.S. military and economic aid, but relations were frequently strained by accusations in Washington that Pakistan was not doing enough to dismantle militant safe havens.

Pakistani officials have long rejected those claims, saying the country’s military operations in tribal regions and elsewhere targeted extremist groups at great human and financial cost.

Musharraf said U.S. policy toward Pakistan has often been inconsistent, with Washington relying on Islamabad during crises but criticizing it when political pressure rises at home.

Analysts say the former president’s comments reflect a longstanding grievance among Pakistan’s military and political leadership: that Pakistan’s cooperation with the United States has not translated into sustained diplomatic trust or long-term economic assistance.

Relations between the two countries have shifted in recent years, especially after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021. While counterterrorism cooperation continues in some areas, the partnership is no longer as central to U.S. foreign policy as it was during the height of the war in Afghanistan.

Musharraf maintained that Pakistan remains vital to regional stability and should be treated as a strategic partner rather than a temporary ally.

“Without Pakistan’s cooperation, there can be no lasting peace in the region,” he said. “Support for Pakistan is support for stability.”

## Musharraf Says Pakistan Was “Abandoned” After Soviet-Afghan War, Sees Little Change Under Obama

Former Pakistani president Pervez Musharraf has argued that Pakistan’s troubled relationship with the United States is rooted in what he describes as Washington’s abandonment of Islamabad after the Soviet-Afghan war, and he said U.S. policy toward Pakistan has remained largely unchanged under President Barack Obama.

In an interview, Musharraf said Pakistan played a central role in the U.S.-backed effort to defeat Soviet forces in Afghanistan during the 1980s, serving as a frontline state for the flow of money, weapons and fighters into the Afghan resistance. But once the Soviets withdrew and the Cold War wound down, he argued, Washington lost interest in the region and left Pakistan to deal with the consequences.

According to Musharraf, that period helped create many of the security problems Pakistan later faced, including militancy, extremism and the destabilizing effects of the Afghan conflict spilling across the border. He suggested that Pakistan was left with armed groups, refugees and a radicalized environment while the United States moved on to other priorities.

Musharraf’s criticism reflects a long-standing Pakistani grievance: that the country was treated as a useful ally during moments of American strategic need, only to be sanctioned or sidelined afterward. Many Pakistani officials and analysts have pointed to the post-1989 period, when U.S. attention shifted away from Afghanistan and sanctions were imposed on Pakistan over its nuclear program, as a turning point in bilateral mistrust.

The former military ruler also said he saw little substantive difference in U.S. policy toward Pakistan after Obama entered the White House. While Obama’s administration promised a broader regional approach to Afghanistan and Pakistan, Musharraf argued that the basic American posture—pressuring Pakistan to do more against militants while questioning its reliability—remained consistent with previous administrations.

He criticized what he viewed as a failure by Washington to fully acknowledge Pakistan’s sacrifices in the fight against terrorism. Pakistan, he said, had suffered extensive casualties among civilians and security forces and faced repeated attacks inside its own borders. Yet, in his view, the country was still often portrayed in Washington as part of the problem rather than as a partner bearing a heavy cost.

Musharraf’s comments come against the backdrop of a complicated U.S.-Pakistan relationship shaped by cooperation, suspicion and competing interests. After the September 11 attacks, Pakistan became a key U.S. ally in the campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Under Musharraf’s leadership, Islamabad provided logistical support, intelligence cooperation and access to supply routes for U.S. forces in Afghanistan.

But tensions persisted. American officials frequently accused Pakistan of tolerating or supporting militant networks that operated across the Afghan border, while Pakistani leaders accused the United States of disregarding Pakistan’s security concerns, especially its rivalry with India and fears of instability in Afghanistan.

Under Obama, the United States intensified drone strikes in Pakistan’s tribal areas and expanded pressure on Islamabad to target militant sanctuaries. At the same time, Washington approved significant military and civilian aid packages, including efforts to strengthen Pakistan’s economy and institutions. Still, mistrust deepened over issues such as drone attacks, the raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad in 2011, and the future of Afghanistan.

Musharraf’s argument is likely to resonate with audiences in Pakistan who believe the United States has repeatedly pursued short-term strategic goals in the region without addressing the long-term fallout. Critics of Musharraf, however, may point out that his own government played a major role in shaping Pakistan’s post-9/11 security policies and that Pakistan’s military establishment has long been accused of maintaining links with militant groups as instruments of regional influence.

The former president’s remarks underscore the enduring divide between Pakistani and American narratives about the Afghan wars. For Washington, Pakistan has often been viewed as an indispensable but frustrating partner. For many in Pakistan, the United States is seen as an unreliable ally whose policies have contributed to the instability it later demanded Pakistan contain.

Musharraf maintained that any durable U.S.-Pakistan partnership would require Washington to recognize Pakistan’s security concerns, respect its sovereignty and acknowledge the historical burden Islamabad says it inherited after the Soviet-Afghan conflict. Without that shift, he suggested, changes in American leadership—from one administration to the next—would make little difference.
